item.title: His and Hers Hippocampus? Sex Differences in the Aging Brain
item.description:
Neuroscience

His and Hers Hippocampus? Sex Differences in the Aging Brain

Subregions of the hippocampus atrophy at different rates for females and males.

Posted July 10, 2026

Key points
  • The hippocampus is an important area of the brain for forming memories.
  • The volume of most subregions of the hippocampus begins to decrease around 50 years of age.
  • Females exhibited a decline in hippocampal volume earlier in life compared to males.
  • Sex differences are important to consider in aging research.

This post was co-authored by Jillian H. Graham, B.S., Justin M. Palmer, Ph.D., & Scott M. Hayes, Ph.D.

What is the hippocampus?

The hippocampus is an area of the brain that is central to forming some of our most important memories that come from our daily experiences. These memories range from landmark life events, such as your best friend’s wedding ceremony, to more mundane events, such as running errands around town.

The hippocampus is vulnerable to age-related structural and functional decline, which contributes to memory difficulties in older adulthood. For example, previous studies have shown that hippocampal volume declines with age (Wolf et al., 2015), which may be associated with greater difficulties on memory tasks (O’Shea et al., 2016). The hippocampus is also one of the first regions to accumulate Alzheimer’s disease pathology, which can further exacerbate hippocampal decline and cognitive impairment.

Additionally, sex differences in hippocampal volumes are often not examined, leading to a lack of understanding of how these structures may vary by biological sex. This lack of knowledge is important to consider given that females are at a higher risk for Alzheimer’s disease compared to males. Therefore, understanding potential sex differences in hippocampal volume may have implications for early detection and intervention of age-related cognitive decline or Alzheimer’s disease.

Hippocampal subfields labeled with different colors. DG = dentate gyrus
Source: Brain image generated using FreeSurfer software.

Segmenting the hippocampus

The hippocampus is not a uniform structure. It consists of several key subregions, called “subfields,” that play unique roles in memory functioning. Limitations in the resolution of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans often impede characterization of hippocampal subfields. Think of this problem as needing a higher-resolution microscope to see small objects in daily life. Fortunately, improvements in neuroimaging technology now allow researchers to measure these different hippocampal subfields. A recently published study with over 200 participants across the adult lifespan (21-87 years old) has demonstrated novel findings on how different areas of the hippocampus are associated with age and biological sex.

Study participants underwent an ultra-high-resolution MRI scan. This may sound invasive, but undergoing these types of scans is harmless! The participant lies on the table, and the scanner takes pictures of the brain. Participants also completed several cognitive tests to measure memory, attention, processing speed, and executive functions. A subgroup of females completed a reproductive questionnaire to measure age of first menstrual cycle, age of menopause, and reproductive span.

This study had several important findings:

  • There were different ages at which the volume began to be significantly lower for each hippocampal subregion. Most areas show significantly lower volume around age 50, but an area referred to as CA2/3 may begin to decline slightly later in life, closer to age 57.
  • Lower volume began earlier for females in the dentate gyrus, a region that is important for separating similar memories, and the CA1 region. However, once lower volume reduction was observed in older males, the age-related volume loss appeared more accelerated relative to females
  • Volumes of the CA1 and dentate gyrus were positively associated with attention scores. However, this same relationship was not observed with memory scores.
  • In females, a younger age of first menstrual cycle was associated with a larger volume in the presubiculum, a region referred to as the “navigation and map-making” hub of the brain.

What are the implications of this research?

The study by Hall and colleagues improves our understanding of age- and sex-related differences in the hippocampus. Their findings may be useful in establishing the age at which hippocampal subfields begin to shrink, which appears to be closer to middle age.

The authors suggested that lower volumes within the hippocampus among females may be related to decreases in estradiol levels, the most potent type of estrogen found in the body. Estrogen is known to directly interact with the hippocampus and can benefit its functioning. However, compared to males, females have a more rapid decline. Males generally have a gradual, slight decline in estradiol as they age, whereas females have a more rapid decline in estradiol during the onset of menopause, which is around the same age at which declines in hippocampal volume were observed. Therefore, the loss of estrogen at these ages may diminish its neuroprotective effects on the hippocampus for females.

Older adults reminiscing
Source: Vitaly Gariev / Unsplash

Volume within certain areas of the hippocampus predicted performance on attention tasks, but not on memory tasks. This was somewhat surprising, given that the hippocampus is well-known to support memory function. The authors explained this finding by noting that attention may help facilitate adequate memory functioning. In other words, attention skills can impact the ability to learn and remember information.

Even though it is easy to think about lower brain volume in older adults relative to younger adults as a decline, it’s important to note that this research study was not longitudinal. Longitudinal studies evaluate the same participants over time, which allows scientists to measure true change in brain structure. Studies such as the one from Hall and colleagues took a snapshot of hippocampal volumes at one point in time across individuals of different ages, which limits the ability to conclude that there was actual decline over time.

Overall, these findings highlight that hippocampal subfields may have differential sensitivity to the effects of aging. While more research is needed to determine potential interventions, such as hormone-based treatments, and how they could help preserve hippocampal structure, these findings emphasize the importance of considering biological sex in aging research for early detection and prevention of decline.

item.title: Remote Work Hurts Early Careers More Than AI
item.description:
Career

Remote Work Hurts Early Careers More Than AI

New data shows physical distance is the bigger threat to entry-level roles.

Posted July 10, 2026

Key points
  • Data across four nations reveals that remote work, not AI alone, caused the recent collapse in junior hiring.
  • Remote work designs can drastically increase management burdens for entry-level roles.
  • Flexible remote options lead to retaining experienced workers longer, which can reduce junior hiring
  • Structured training can effectively offset the loss of casual office learning.

Although it has never been easy for everyone to start a career, there is a measurable decline in early career roles, especially for recent graduates. In recent years, public concern has focused heavily on generative AI, with many fearing that automation software will completely replace entry-level office roles.

While it is easy to assume AI will hollow out office jobs the way automation once transformed the manufacturing sector, the evidence is mixed at best. Instead, recent economic data suggests that the drop in junior hiring is deeply tied to physical distance from the office.

Moving away from shared physical workspaces has disrupted how new hires learn, connect, and find mentors, hitting remote-friendly work sectors the hardest.

The Broken Career Ladder

Starting in late 2022, entry-level job opportunities fell sharply across developed nations, particularly in white-collar fields like software engineering and professional services.

While AI gets the blame, a landmark 2026 study by economists Peter John Lambert and Yannick Schindler paints a different picture. They tracked 243 million hires and 407 million online job postings across the U.S., UK, Canada, and Australia from 2017 to 2025.

When analyzed on its own, AI exposure seems to hurt junior hiring. However, when you look at AI exposure and remote work trends together, the independent effect of AI disappears. The research indicates that entry-level hiring collapsed primarily because highly digital roles are now disproportionately done from home.

Remote Work Changes Management Demands

Why does shifting a role to the home environment paralyze junior hiring? The economic data points to a shift in how companies manage risk, coupled with a major change in workforce demographics.

First, the stakes of a bad hire are significantly higher in a remote setup. In a physical office, a struggling junior employee can be redirected quickly through casual, daily course corrections. In isolation, however, mistakes go unnoticed longer, take more effort to fix, and disrupt digital workflows more.

When remote setups increase the management burden, the short-term benefits of hiring experience, especially for time-stretched managers, often take priority over the long-term benefits of training and development. Instead of investing in long-term development, companies are raising their hiring standards to recruit independent, senior workers who require less daily oversight. Because the cost of mistakes is higher when people work in isolation, hiring experienced talent is simply a lower-risk option.

Second, remote work has altered the supply of senior talent. Flexible arrangements have made it much easier and more desirable for older, highly experienced professionals to delay retirement. Many older and experienced professionals who can work independently without oversight are choosing to stay in the workforce longer, and without the draining daily commute. Faced with an independent expert on one side and a costly training risk on the other, hiring managers often choose experience.

How New Workers Learn

To understand why physical isolation stalls early-career development, it helps to explain how skills and capability are developed over the course of someone’s career. Research by Xiao Ma, Alejandro Nakab, and Daniela Vidart (2026) explains that professional learning is driven by two distinct sources:

  1. Internal learning (absorbing knowledge from coworkers)
  2. External learning (formal, structured on-the-job training)

Young employees rely heavily on casual, face-to-face interactions with more experienced colleagues because they are an easy, low-cost way to pick up skills. Remote environments disrupt this organic process.

According to social learning theory, developing professional competence requires active observation and behavioral modeling. A junior employee does not just pick up technical mechanics through proximity; they must actively witness how a senior peer navigates a high-stakes mistake, de-escalates an upset client, or structures an ambiguous argument. In a remote setup, this crucial first step of behavioral attention is entirely blocked because a new employee cannot model behaviors that they are never in the room to see.

Crucially, Ma, Nakab, and Vidart’s model highlights that well-structured, formal training can partially offset these internal learning losses. The more remote an environment is, the more vital structured external training becomes to bridge the gap.

Designing Better Hybrid Systems

To protect the next generation of talent, organizations must move away from unstructured “choose-your-own-days” hybrid schedules and design clear, intentional frameworks.

1. Coordinated Office Schedules

Teams should coordinate their schedules to maximize overlapping office hours. These shared days should be preserved for collaborative activities: team meetings, group training, mentoring, and social connection. Conversely, remote days can prioritize quiet, focused, individual tasks.

2. Structured Hybrid Onboarding

Onboarding must focus on building real relationships. While virtual onboarding works well for paperwork and IT setup, in-person time is essential for understanding company culture and gaining role clarity. Research shows that structured onboarding helps new hires reach full productivity up to two months faster. When this is not possible in person, it should be clearly planned and structured to build connections with formal and informal activities.

3. Formal Mentorship Programs

Because remote work makes informal mentoring difficult, companies must formalize the process. Effective programs need a clear timeline (6 to 12 months) and a regular meeting schedule (like biweekly sessions). Both sides need support: mentors need basic coaching tips, and mentees should be taught how to prepare agendas and ask for specific feedback.

A Complex Labor Market

Ultimately, the world of work is shaped by many forces acting at once. Digital automation is altering tasks, remote work is changing workplace dynamics, and economic shifts are reshaping hiring budgets and company missions. Cultural changes are also changing the way people interpret their relationships with each other and with work.

As the data reminds us, we cannot point to a single culprit like AI to explain the challenges facing early-career workers. Rebuilding and maintaining a resilient talent pipeline means actively creating entry-level opportunities. It also means accepting that, when it comes to early-career development, remote work can do more harm than good.

item.title: Do The Thing You Think You Can't
item.description:
Self-Help

Do The Thing You Think You Can't

Personal Perspective: How to break free from whatever is holding you back.

Posted July 10, 2026

Key points
  • Negative experiences can hold us back, but we can break free.
  • Realize that old beliefs are not necessarily truths—change is possible.
  • Setbacks are opportunities for growth.
  • Having the courage to try something that scares us can transform our lives.
Source: Tracy Strauss

Especially during difficult times, it’s important to have an outlet, a stress reliever, or simply an activity in which we can express ourselves freely. Studies have shown that regular exercise can boost mood. For many, however, exercise can be a struggle, and it can take some doggedness to get going.

I didn’t think I could “Zumba.”

I was 40 years old. I knew I was fit enough for the one-hour Latin-inspired dance fitness class at the gym because I took other cardio classes, from cycling to boot camp to kickboxing. I considered myself relatively fit. But I didn’t think I could take a Zumba class. I didn’t think I could allow my body to move expressively. I didn’t think I could bear to see my reflection in the mirror.

Negative Experiences Shape Us

My past was dictating my present.

When I was five, every weekend my mother put a Disney album on the record player, and I skipped and hopped and leaped around the room for hours, paying attention to nothing and no one but the music and the way I expressed myself through my body. I danced; I lived and breathed the rhythm of each moment, until the sexual abuse of my childhood caused me to stop.

I grew up ashamed of my body, closing it up, folding myself inward, so that no one would see my pain or what was underneath it: the essence of me. As an adult, I spent years in therapy psychologically processing the various aspects and effects of the abuse, peeling away the layers, but my body still stored the unspeakable parts of my past.

Break Free From Old Beliefs

Despite whatever has happened to us, whatever beliefs we form around events and their aftermath, we can transform our thoughts and our way of life—though it can be difficult, doggedness can help us through.

On Sundays at the gym, I could see the Zumba class from the step master machine. Weekly, for almost a year, as I climbed on the machine, I watched the Zumba class through the studio glass walls, wanting to be like the women inside, women of all different shapes, sizes, ages, and physical abilities, who moved their bodies so freely, so expressively. They danced combinations of cumbia, merengue, samba, and other routines choreographed and led by Adam, the instructor I overheard a trainer call “the epitome of life force.”

One day, I couldn’t stop myself: I went into the studio. Nervous, I stood in the back of the room so as not to be noticed making what I anticipated would be a fool of myself. I’d left my contact lenses at home so that I wouldn’t be able to see myself in the mirror, but I could still make out the shape of my body in the distance, my purple tank top, my black workout capris, my blonde hair up in a ponytail. I felt my legs and arms and insides shaking.

The instructor, Adam, walked in front of the mirrors. “If it’s your first time taking Zumba,” he said, “just keep moving and have fun. Don’t worry about knowing what you’re doing.”

Then he started the music: Ariana Grande’s “Break Free.”

I spent the class (and many, many more) in the back of the room, feeling uncoordinated and embarrassed, at times panicked by the sudden rush of chills and tears that released as my body moved. I shut my eyes and felt the music—I’m stronger than I’ve been before!/This is the part when I break free/’Cause I can’t resist it no more! I felt my five-year-old self inside my skin, dancing: I found my own lost joy.

Adam gave us tips about posture, showed us how to hold our shoulders and chest open, how to move our feet and our legs. “Do you feel sexy?” he shouted. The body was not an object to be debased, but a birthright to be respected and honored.

My body, so used to walking around closed and clamped down, started to open. As I continued going to Zumba class, I slowly made my way from the back of the studio towards the front of the room. Outside of class, I became aware that I was beginning to carry myself differently.

Overcome Setbacks

When we take a big step and make a change, that doesn’t mean it will all be smooth sailing.

Three months after I stepped into my first Zumba class, I had a setback. Watching the television news, I learned that a man had been arrested at a popular local café, where he was later convicted of videotaping women in the restroom. He’d hidden electronic devices in a fake flower basket and filmed and streamed nude images of patrons onto his cell phone.

I’d been at the café on the dates of the crime. I’d stopped in during a bike ride to use the restroom. I’d seen the flower basket. When I saw the news report, my heart began to pound, and then I went numb. The trauma of my past came flooding back.

I called the police.

The following day, the Zumba class was on my schedule, but I wasn’t sure I could go. I considered staying home, sitting it out. All I could think about was the man at the café. I didn’t want anyone to see my body, my “booty.” I didn’t think I could bear to show myself in the world ever again. I didn’t want to feel the pain.

I went to class anyway. I contemplated standing in the back, in the corner, out of sight, out of mind. But then I didn’t. I walked straight to my newfound space, three rows from the front, near the speakers.

When Adam turned on the music, I saw my reflection in the mirror, and for a moment, I felt paralyzed, haunted, watched, and violated. But then, I started to dance. I felt myself break free. I felt my joie de vivre. And I understood that no one could take that away from me.

Source: Tracy Strauss

Turn Challenges Into Opportunities

When life gives you lemons, make lemonade.

I never imagined that my decision to finally step inside a Zumba class would lead me to become a Zumba instructor. In middle school, I was the girl who auditioned for the kickline and cheerleading teams, didn’t make the cut, and was made fun of by the popular kids.

At 42, I told myself I had nothing to lose. I obtained my Zumba instructor license and auditioned for jobs at local gyms, where I was hired. Almost a decade later, weekly, I get up on a stage in front of a room of people, and I turn on the lights and the fans and the music, and we all shake off our week and our booty.

In a time of great turmoil, it’s important to take a pause to forget about life for a while and just let loose. Immerse yourself in the moment. Be in flow. Do the thing you think you can’t. Take up space, be yourself, doggedly, in whatever way that brings you happiness.

item.title: Got Heat? Cold? Wildfires? Droughts? Hurricanes?
item.description:
Environment

Got Heat? Cold? Wildfires? Droughts? Hurricanes?

Three ways to sustainably engage with the climate crisis.

Posted July 10, 2026

Key points
  • A majority of people care about the environmental and health impacts of climate change, but struggle to act.
  • Structural, cultural and psychological barriers impede our ability to focus on the climate crisis.
  • Slightly modifying our lifestyles by allowing more quiet time, rest time, and emotional honesty is key.
  • Individual engagement drives collective action.

This summer, England's temperatures reached 99.9 degrees Fahrenheit, the highest June temperature on record in the UK. A heat wave triggered a "red heat health alert" at exactly the same time the city of London was hosting its 8th annual Climate Week. The irony here is obvious.

The British experienced cascading climate disruptions—nature's reminders to wake the heck up. The sweltering temperatures cut off vital transportation services, closed schools and businesses, and caused hospitals to restrict services as they struggled to cope with an influx of heat-related demands.

Beneath the immediate chaos, an urgent question looms: Can the British look up, notice, and care—even after these hot days finally pass? Can any of us?

As a psychotherapist working at the intersection of climate and mental health, I spend a good deal of time tracking emotional and behavioral responses to climate change across the globe. A new Yale Program on Climate Change Communication (YPCCC) poll reveals that a solid majority of Americans (65%) say that global warming is personally important to them. Yet, there is a high level of cognitive dissonance (or conflicting thoughts, feelings, and behaviors) as people struggle to reconcile fears, worries, grief, and hopes with ordinary life.

What I see happening in England, and many other countries, is something the YPCCC has called the "attitude-behavior gap." This is the fancy term for the very real discrepancy between human concern and climate action engagement. As YPCCC research indicates, even amongst those most willing to act (51%), few actually engage in political actions to limit global warming (6-16%), such as contacting government officials, attending protests, and signing petitions. This attitude-behavior gap is deeply problematic because human behavior tilts towards complacency at a time when climate collapse is accelerating.

What if we could harness the collective energy of the 89% global majority—who indeed want their governments to act—and effectively intensify collective pressure on world governments, institutions and businesses?

Here in the U.S., America's natural resources—including air, water, and public lands—are in jeopardy under the Trump administration, which has rolled back environmental protections and clean energy investments. This is precisely the moment that human concern for the environment and human health ought to be vocalized (ad nauseam) to build public pressure demanding government response.

In my clinical work, I've found that giving folks language for understanding the psychological mechanisms and structural barriers they encounter when it comes to the climate crisis is a helpful way of unsticking their psyches. Although there are many such barriers, a few key ones worth noting are: Noise, Depletion, and Intellectualization.

Noise

Noise is a catch-all for busy people leading busy lives—and/or oppressed and marginalized people leading oppressed and marginalized lives. Our busy-ness is no accident—it's by design. The inherent expectations of capitalism—efficiency, productivity, economic growth, and consumerism—effectively grind, entrap and distract us. Capitalism, as right-wing strategist Steve Bannon has identified, is an effective engine for breeding collective complacency ("flood the zone with sh*t)."

If we're honest with ourselves, can we admit that it's easy to be lulled into a state of submission, or remain frozen, or numb, entranced by a Pied-Piper-like spell that tells us to "keep looking away" rather than face the existential elephant in the room?

Just because people are distracted by noise does not mean that they don't care about climate change. People tend to assume that others around them don't care about the climate crisis, but this simply isn't true. A "perception gap" exists in which people tend to underestimate their fellow citizens' concern for the environment. In fact, polls consistently show that the majority of the global population does, indeed, want climate action and would even make personal sacrifices to help.

Additionally, a large segment of folks who care deeply about ecological destruction is too busy working jobs, feeding families, and eking out survival to have space or bandwidth to engage. The cost of living crisis suppresses the ability to act. In the U.S., notoriously sparse family-friendly policies (e.g. paid maternity/paternity leave, affordable healthcare and childcare) mean that that less resourced folks are overburdened with day to day concerns. Meanwhile, the middle class is kept saturated and distracted by a culture of consumerism. For those of us who are able to cut through this Noise, it is our responsibility to act.

Depletion

Depletion is a physical and emotional state of "running on empty" that stems from ambient Noise. It turns out that, eventually, living with constant over-stimulation and too little rest catches up with you. Long workdays. Second or third jobs. Cost-of-living struggles. Intense careers that don't allow you to clock out at the end of a long day. And, of course, the glaze-eyed exhaustion from the most demanding relationship of all—your smartphone.

The pings. The posts. The likes. The feeds. The shares. Smartphones demand our constant attention from the moment we wake up to the moment we go to sleep. A pervasive cloud hangs over our heads of "I just can't keep up" that leaves us feeling ragged at the end of each day. Burnout, at least in the US, is difficult to avoid.

Living in a depleted state is not healthy for anyone, including children, nor will it help tackle our climate crisis. To stay depleted means kicking the existential can further and further down the street -- rather than picking it up ourselves. A depleted society is not in any shape to look after its future generations.

Intellectualization

Perhaps the most subtle barrier to climate engagement is Intellectualization -- an interesting form of mental gymnastics subconsciously adopted to insulate people from the emotional pain of the climate crisis. On one hand, people are honest about the hard realities of the climate crisis, but on the other, climate emotions are kept at arm's length. When we shield ourselves from pain, heartache, fear, anger, etc., then we deny the emotional gravity of the situation. Yet, emotions are actually portals to motivation, care and engagement. By keeping those doors shut, we pay a price.

These are only three barriers to climate engagement. But keep in mind that Noise, Depletion, and Intellectualization are temporary traps. With intention, we can move past them and carve a path forward that will be meaningful, productive, and clarifying. This is the hope of climate behavioral change.

Simple Solutions

To combat noise, seek quiet. Try to spend time in quiet spaces—like libraries, book stores, museums, parks, forests, beaches or public gardens. Create a quiet zone in your home—for example, a porch, a seat near a window, a corner of a room that is discussed and agreed upon—or use a pair of noise-canceling headphones. Perhaps you set up some comfy pillows or put a sign up on the wall to designate a quiet space. If you live with others, consider creating an agreement to honor quiet hours each day (e.g., early morning, before bedtime). Consider making this quiet time device-free as well.

Building Quiet time back into our lives reminds us to slow down, reconnect with our thoughts and feelings, and to replenish ourselves. One of my clients starts each morning on his balcony with tea, another unwinds on her rooftop at the end of the day, watching the sunset. Granting our brains some breathing room will help us to internally settle and regroup, so that we stay connected to ourselves, and our values and priorities. And it keeps us sane, too.

To combat depletion, try replenishment. Dr. Saundra Dalton-Smith has identified 7 types of rest that every person needs (and it involves more than kicking your feet up at the end of the day). Yes, she mentions physical rest and mental rest. But she goes further, including sensory rest (i.e., shutting out overwhelming stimuli), emotional rest (i.e., honestly expressing your feelings), social rest (i.e., setting boundaries around toxic relationships), and spiritual rest (i.e., connecting to something larger than yourself). If ever there were a prescription for our current existential woes, it is this! We can't tackle climate change if we are not reasonably well-rested.

To combat Intellectualization, try emotional composting in your community or with a buddy or professional. We spend a lot of time avoiding our feelings because we're afraid of them and worry that they will consume us. In fact, it's just the opposite: our avoidant tendencies drive up inner tension and distress. The only way to experience relief is by honestly sharing our feelings. When we share our feelings with others, it's even more beneficial because we discover that we are not alone, and we can feel validated, and even motivated by one another. Emotional composting is a process of breaking down messy complex emotions into identifiable ones so that we move towards greater emotional attunement. From there, it's easier to act.

In order to effectively respond to the mounting climate emergency that generates heat waves, triggers extreme weather events and pushes us past dangerous planetary tipping points, then we must activate our quiet attention, we must find ways to replenish ourselves physically, emotionally and spiritually, and we must sit with our emotions in an honest way. This is a basic global prescription, regardless of where you are located.

When we understand the forces that keep us from acting—Noise! Depletion! Intellectualization! -- we can stop running in the same tired, predictable circles that perpetuate avoidance. And we can collectively address the climate crisis rather than leave it up to climate activists, professionals, and frontline communities. Our planet and younger generations desperately need us to wake up, stay vigilant, and act in alignment with our eco-concern. Now, more than ever. As humans, we have the power to modify our behaviors—and we can start today.

item.title: Burnout Isn't Always About Working Too Much
item.description:
Burnout

Burnout Isn't Always About Working Too Much

5 overlooked habits that quietly fuel chronic stress and exhaustion.

Posted July 10, 2026

Source: Andrei Askirka/Shutterstock

Did you know that a fire burning out often produces more visible smoke than a fire burning at its peak? Burnout works in much the same way. Before the flame goes out, there are often smoke signals we overlook. Recognizing them cues us that it’s time to rethink how we're approaching our workdays.

Several known workplace issues lead to burnout: the culture of an organization, workload, lack of control, unfairness, and inadequate support. In my clinical experience, there are also interpersonal and cognitive patterns that can intensify feelings of burnout, especially in highly capable professionals. Actual workload only tells part of the story, sometimes it’s also the emotional weight we’re carrying from the habits we bring to work that are adding to our exhaustion.

These habits, drawn from principles I discuss in my book Beyond Happiness: The 6 Secrets of Lifetime Satisfaction, (Guttman, 2023), fall into five patterns of behavior:

  1. Assuming Responsibility For Everything

Many capable people feel a sense of ownership for work that may fall outside of their job responsibilities. As a result, we micro-manage, or feel a sense of hyper-responsibility for everyone’s work. This leads to chronic work vigilance, an overloaded brain, resentment, and mood swings. “If I don’t do it, it won’t get done,” is the code we live by. It’s that code that is exacerbating our burnout. This code is based on an assumption, not reality.

Pausing and recognizing what can be delegated is key. We need to focus on tolerating the discomfort of sitting with the anxiety of not being in constant control. Try these exercises. Challenge yourself to delegate one task a day and build from there. Take a 10-minute break in the middle of the day. Put a boundary around lunchtime, so your brain can reboot and you can eat. Break the habit of assuming responsibility that was never really yours and you will be making one step forward in reducing burnout.

  1. People-Pleasing Instead of Setting Boundaries

We often think about people-pleasing as a behavior we do with family members and friends, but I have also seen this frequently in work environments. Fear of disappointing others exists everywhere. We want reinforcement for our work product, so we work longer than we should or take on someone else’s work seeking that approval. Then resentment starts to build as we fear setting boundaries that may disrupt the desire for approval. The likelihood that a manager or co-worker will recognize and call out our hard work is slight. Since, as humans, we harbor a negativity bias (Vaish et al., 2008), we put the lack of feedback from managers in the “negative” feedback column. However, silence is just “neutral.” It’s not good or bad. This leaves us emotionally exhausted, chasing validation, leading to feelings of chronic stress and burnout. You can try these strategies. Say “no” unapologetically to one thing every day no matter how small. You will see with time that your relationships at work don’t change. This will build confidence; your identity won’t be tied to being helpful at work, and the boundaries you’ve set will contribute to a reduction in burnout.

  1. Avoiding Difficult Conversations That Only Become Harder Over Time

Conflict avoidance at work may reduce your anxiety temporarily. However, since you’re only putting off the inevitable, your anxiety will continue to increase over time. This leads to a constant state of anticipatory anxiety. Frequently, when we are avoiding talking to someone, it’s because we’ve played out the entire conversation in our heads, catastrophizing the outcome. The problem with having this back-and-forth conversation with ourselves instead of the actual person is that it can inadvertently put a strain on the relationship since we’ve anticipated a negative outcome. Think back on a situation where you avoided a conversation. Once you had it, did it go the way you thought it would? I doubt it. I imagine it went much better. Another case of negativity bias. Instead of creating weeks or months of stress at work, which adds to feeling burned out, challenge yourself to a date and time for the conversation. Tell someone you’re going to do it, so you have built-in accountability. Relief will replace anticipation, reducing your overall anxiety and helping with burnout.

  1. Living with Chronic Indecision

Many of us struggle with making decisions and suffer from analysis paralysis. We believe there is a right or wrong choice. However, with most decisions, the answer falls somewhere in a grey area, where both choices are “right,” and trying to analyze which choice your manager “wants” you to make will always ultimately come down to an educated guess. Making decisions at work demonstrates confidence. Asking someone else to decide for you shows insecurity. When you’re wracked with anxiety and fear, compulsively weighing options or needing decision confirmation, work output slows down. Most managers prefer you make decisions and move on, even if you have to change one or two of them. Chronic decision paralysis contributes to feelings of burnout. Challenge yourself to make one decision a day, no matter how small. Once that becomes less intimidating, continue to build from there.

  1. Never Acknowledging What You've Accomplished Before Moving Onto the Next Task

It’s critical that you pause and reflect at work on the projects you’ve completed. Then give yourself the praise you deserve. You can’t rely on your manager remembering to tell you, “Job well done.” You need to do this for yourself. If we don’t reflect on our “wins” and just move onto the next task, we can feel taken advantage of or taken for granted in the workplace. You’d be surprised how many of my clients find this personal reflection to be useful even though you’re acknowledging yourself. When you move the goal post every time you accomplish something, your brain never receives the reward signal that something has been completed. Instead of alternating between effort and recovery, you get stuck in continuous striving. This can make you prone to burnout since you never give your nervous system permission to recover. Without recovery time, we eventually become less focused, less creative, and less resilient. The time you give yourself doesn’t have to be long, it just has to be intentional.

Sometimes recovering from burnout isn't about working fewer hours. It's about recognizing the "smoke signals," the hidden habits that quietly add to your exhaustion. Once you identify them, you can begin changing the behaviors that fuel them. As you break these patterns, work becomes one part of your life rather than the force that defines it, and your life begins to feel like your own again.

item.title: Cultural Identity and Well-Being
item.description:
Cross-Cultural Psychology

Cultural Identity and Well-Being

Culture refers to "shared, learned behavior and meanings" and affects thriving.

Posted July 10, 2026

Key points
  • Beliefs, values, ethnicity, and where you’ve lived comprise your cultural identity.
  • When culture is in sync with well-being, positivity and resilience are enhanced.
  • Cultural variability still has to satisfy the reality of liveability.
  • Cultural diversity brings together different talents and skills, which increases productivity.

“If we are to achieve a richer culture, rich in contrasting values, we must recognize the whole gamut of human potentialities, and so weave a less arbitrary social fabric, one in which each diverse human gift will find a fitting place.” — Margaret Mead

Why is culture so important? So influential? How can we understand the value of accepting the diversity of culture?

The term “culture” commonly refers to ‘shared, learned behavior and meanings’ among certain groups of people and provides a framework through which individuals can make sense of their world (1).

Cultural Identity

Your beliefs, values, ethnicity, where you’ve lived before, and where you live now all comprise your cultural identity. When arriving in a new country, it is likely that the culture’s beliefs and values may differ from those of your home country.

This transition to your new country may be difficult, not only for you but also for the new people you will meet. You are trying to hold on to what you value and believe, and this might clash with your new culture, which consists of different values and beliefs.

Differences in ethnicity usually include differences in language. Your appearance, eating habits, clothing, and lifestyle may also be very different than those in your new country. All these adaptations will be challenging for you, but also for those people you meet who struggle with diversity.

Acceptance and nonjudgment are the keys to success. You will have to accept certain differences in your new culture and avoid judgment. Likewise, the new people you meet may reciprocate by accepting and being nonjudgmental of you.

When these things happen, your hybrid cultural identity will kick in. Your well-being and new identity in this cultural setting will be shaped by how long the assimilation process takes. The sooner you feel at home, the healthier your new cultural identity will feel.

“No culture can live if it attempts to be exclusive.” — Mahatma Gandhi

Effects on Well-Being

Well-being is the state of thriving (not just surviving) across various areas of life, such as relationships, work, play, and more, despite ups and downs. Culture and well-being are inextricably aligned.

Cultural involvement includes maintaining your heritage and an appreciation of the arts. Well-being benefits include a connection to your roots, an affiliation with your family and ethnic history, and a supportive connection to your identity of origin.

When one’s culture is in sync with one’s well-being, positivity and resilience are enhanced while loneliness and cognitive decline are reduced. Indigenous communities are especially vulnerable to any disconnect from their cultural heritage, mainly because of the absence of outside influences and the long history of traditional values and beliefs.

"The culture of a workplace—an organization’s values, norms and practices—has a huge impact on our happiness and success." — Adam Grant

Liveability

There can be significant challenges to your well-being when arriving in a new culture. Cultural variability still has to satisfy the reality of liveability.

That is, certain human conditions will lead to a person’s thriving or lack thereof. This often means that the values, norms, and social relationships of a new culture are seen as liveable.

When these conditions of liveability are not being met, a person’s well-being will be at risk. This concept becomes more real when faced with experiences of discrimination, bullying, or social bias.

The liveability within such cultures becomes compromised. This does not only apply to living in a new country. One’s liveability acceptance could apply to any new workplace, new school, or new community.

"Diversity: the art of thinking independently together." — Malcolm Forbes

The Values of Diversity

Cultural diversity brings together different talents and skills, which increases productivity. We learn from each other’s experiences and apply this new awareness to our own lives. Diverse minds working together create solutions by drawing on different ways of thinking and perspectives. Creativity gets a boost.

Cultural Identity
Source: xiaoxian / Pexels

We learn about other cultures, lifestyles, and ethnicities, which expands our awareness to alternative points of view. Diversity creates a wider spectrum of information and knowledge. A wider spectrum of ideas leads to more creative solutions. Improved cultural insight reduces the negative aspects of diversity, such as racism, homophobia, and sexism.

Simplexity, a recently created term, proposes a possible complementary relationship between complexity and simplicity. The complexity of cultural assimilation appears to be a prime candidate for mechanisms that promote a healthier cultural awareness and community well-being.

Margaret Mead’s quote: “If we are to achieve a richer culture, rich in contrasting values, we must recognize the whole gamut of human potentialities…” summarizes where culture and well-being are genuinely copasetic. In the modern world today, there is an opportunity to create a symbiotic relationship between culture and well-being that promulgates human potential.

item.title: The Use of Games in Therapy: It’s Not Just Fun and Games
item.description:
Therapy

The Use of Games in Therapy: It’s Not Just Fun and Games

Play in therapy has therapeutic benefit and can be a transformative tool.

Posted July 10, 2026

Key points
  • The use of games in treatment is valuable.
  • Therapists approach the use of games in multilayered ways to maximize benefit.
  • There are various types of games and ways of using games effectively in therapy.

Utilizing games in therapy is common for those clinicians who work with children, teens, or families, but sometimes parents may not fully understand the value of games in a therapy setting.

Therapeutic game use can be a highly effective way of engaging clients while simultaneously getting to issues that are part of the presenting problem. They are not just for amusement or a time filler; games and playful activities can be used for action and change.

Source: Ron Lach/Pexels

Why This Approach Can Be a Game-Changer

Therapists who work with families and young people tune into considering intervention methods that go beyond the traditional talking approach expected for most adults for much of a therapy session. While therapy with children sometimes involves direct discussion, inquiry into relevant issues, or teaching of skills, there are times when a playful activity within the context of a session can be highly beneficial. Even very mature or highly verbal children can benefit from a different way to engage, practice social-emotional skills in a pleasurable way, or take a break from highly intense material by shifting gears. Games or playful activities also help signal to a child that the therapy process doesn’t have to be scary or unpleasant.

When games are used therapeutically, they can be an excellent way to lower inhibition, increase engagement, target skills, and add lighthearted positivity when facing sometimes difficult issues. For example, a very shy or socially anxious child may find it easier to answer printed icebreaker-type questions on a card than to engage in direct dialogue to start. For a youngster coping with a parental divorce or a family transition, a game that highlights and validates many of the typical feelings and questions children have can be highly valuable. For a pre-teen struggling with anger or impulse-control difficulties, finding ways to add a playful orientation to building strategies for better behavioral responsiveness can be a game-changer.

Source: Sylvain/Pexels

Types of Games

There are a variety of types of games or toys that might be used therapeutically, and therapists will choose depending on the developmental age, presenting issue, and personality style.

Some games or toys in a therapist’s office might be the type found in any toy store. Utilizing a card game, Nerf basketball, or Jenga blocks allows some playful engagement while working on frustration tolerance, impulse control, and lowering of defensiveness. The game is part of the work, but it is the verbal discussion and processing of various aspects that is likely to be different from what might happen at a family game night. There is a meta-level of processing going on beyond the rules of the game to which the therapist is alerting and utilizing metaphorically.

Sometimes therapists might therapeutically gamify more traditional games in order to add elements of a more psychological nature, such as shifting Go Fish to "Go Fish for a Feeling" (for someone needing practice in understanding emotions) or regular Hangman becomes Coping Hangman (using words from coping tool kit developed during a particular session). Game-like elements tend to increase client engagement, participation, and motivation - while still serving the purpose of increasing exploration, intervention and reinforcement.

Most therapists also have some more therapeutic-type games that need to be purchased at more specialized sites and focus on more targeted skills related to various presenting problems, from anxiety to impulse control to social skills. These prepackaged games allow more specialized focus on psychological issues in a way that is often more child-friendly. Clients seeing themselves in a problem-solving card question in a game or successfully practicing skills learned from a game as in-between session homework can be remarkably impactful.

Some therapists may even create a game or activity with kids that focuses on their particular needs or issues. This allows personalization, taps into creativity, and encourages empowerment for recovery. And the enjoyment is a bonus byproduct.

Source: Natalie Kinnear/Unsplash

Play Therapy and Play in Therapy

Many child clinicians who incorporate play and games into session consider this a form of play therapy, but it is worth noting that there is a specialized field of Play Therapy and certification available as a Registered Play Therapist (RPT).

While broader use of structured activities and games can be utilized by any licensed therapist, RPTs receive specialized training related to processing emotions and healing from trauma. Such therapists often use puppets, sand trays, clay, dolls, or figurines and use play as the primary vehicle for assessment and treatment and look for themes that can indicate more underlying or unconscious information; much of the work is more child-led and unstructured.

Other child therapists might also use puppets or figurines to engage a child and family, but the focus of using play in therapy might be more structured or might be used more periodically rather than consistently as the method of engagement.

Source: Beasternchen/Pixabay

Game Application Beyond Therapy

Games with children or teens in session can be valuable from a therapeutic angle, but families can also benefit from finding time to engage in playful activities together at home. Amidst the busy schedules and necessary household routines, it can be hard to make time for fun and games; however, time playing together can strengthen bonds, allow relaxed moments, foster problem-solving, and make memories. A therapist-type approach is not required nor suggested at home; in fact, the value comes from parents showing up, being present, and engaging playfully with other young humans in the household who matter. This is not just child’s play; this benefits everyone.
